analysis.investment_thesis: Blue Dart is a fine logistics brand but a poor growth investment: revenue CAGR of 9.3% and net profit CAGR of 2.8% over nine years are deeply inadequate, and earnings have been declining for three consecutive years (INR 382 Cr → INR 371 Cr → INR 301 Cr → INR 252 Cr). Paying 44x earnings for a decelerating, DHL-subsidiary business with contracting EBITDA trends violates every principle of rational growth investing.
key_strengths: India's strongest premium express courier brand with unmatched air network — six Boeing 757 freighters and deep penetration
Consistent positive OCF in all 5 years with strong FCF generation (INR 488 Cr in FY25)
Revenue growing at ~10% annually — not exciting but business is not in terminal decline
key_risks: Net profit declining every year since FY22 — the business is losing earnings power despite volume growth
EBITDA trend is contracting over the last 5 years — structural margin pressure from competition and cost inflation
DHL parent ownership (75%) limits strategic freedom; key decisions are made in Singapore, not Mumbai
red_flags: Net profit down 34% from FY22 peak (INR 382 Cr) to FY25 (INR 252 Cr) — three years of consecutive earnings decline
EBITDA has contracted from INR 1,116 Cr (FY21) to INR 894 Cr (FY25) despite 74% revenue growth — cost structure deterioration
P/E of 44x on declining earnings is the definition of value destruction for shareholders
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Blue Dart built a wonderful logistics network over four decades, but from my perspective it has entered a period of financial deterioration that makes it uninvestable at current prices. The dichotomy is striking: revenue has grown from INR 3,288 Cr (FY21) to INR 5,720 Cr (FY25) — a 74% increase — yet EBITDA has fallen from INR 1,116 Cr to INR 894 Cr and net profit from INR 382 Cr to INR 252 Cr. This is a business scaling revenues while destroying margins, the inverse of what I seek.

The DHL parentage is structurally problematic in my framework. Visionary, owner-oriented management is the backbone of long-term growth compounding. A subsidiary answering to a multinational parent lacks the independence to make bold, long-term capital allocation decisions. The company's inability to convert its brand premium into expanding margins amid India's e-commerce logistics boom suggests competitive forces from Delhivery, Ekart, and others are more intense than the stock price implies. Avoid until earnings trajectory reverses convincingly.
